standard.label: Standard form
standard.note: Subtraction only in the six usual pairs (IV, IX, XL, XC, CD, CM); no letter more than three times in a row.
standard.justification: The forms now standard already occur in Roman and medieval material, but stricter modern canonical order is typical chiefly in modern usage.

additive4.label: Additive fours and nines
additive4.note: IIII for 4, VIIII for 9, XXXX for 40, CCCC for 400. Common on Roman inscriptions and in medieval manuscripts; survives on clock faces.
additive4.justification: Additive fours and nines are ordinary in the examined Roman and medieval records and survive in early modern accounts and modern clocks and monuments.
additive4.where: Roman inscriptions and medieval documents. Later examples include clock dials and monuments.

irregularSub.label: Irregular subtraction
irregularSub.note: A smaller letter subtracted from a larger one outside the six usual pairs: IC = 99, IL = 49, XM = 990.
irregularSub.justification: Classical exceptions have narrow scope, and late-fifteenth-century IC is attested in print and stone; a wider period rating for IL or XM lacks equivalent evidence.
irregularSub.where: Check the exact pair. The late medieval evidence includes IC in Italian print and Roman epitaphs.

runSub.label: Repeated subtraction
runSub.note: Several identical letters subtracted together: IIX = 8, XIIX = 18, XXC = 80.
runSub.justification: Flavian IIX and XIIX, Republican XXC, and incunable iic/iiic belong to identifiable traditions, with scarce evidence in the intervening centuries.

oddOrder.label: Letters out of the usual order
oddOrder.note: The letters break the usual descending order; read mechanically, each letter is added unless the next one is larger.
oddOrder.justification: Individually documented exceptions such as classical XXCIII and reported eighth-century LXL support a low prior for named forms, conditional on structure and context.

additiveSum.label: Every letter added
additiveSum.note: This reading adds all the letters. Compare it with readings that use subtraction or multipliers.
additiveSum.justification: Certain lower-before-higher medieval ordinals are additive in Latin word order, but the general method of ignoring order is only a fallback.

multiplicative.label: Superscript multiplier
multiplicative.note: A superscript ᵐ or ᶜ multiplies the number before it: iiᵐ = 2000, vᶜ = 500.
multiplicative.justification: Raised C and M are frequent in some late medieval accounts and attested in sixteenth-century commercial arithmetic and Scottish records.
multiplicative.where: Late medieval accounts and date formulae, early modern commercial arithmetic and Scottish accounts.

multiplicativePlain.label: Multiplier written on the line
multiplicativePlain.note: M or C read as a multiplier although written on the line: IIM = 2000, VC = 500.
multiplicativePlain.justification: Baseline multiplication is reported sporadically for classical thousands and attested in later medieval and early modern evidence, sometimes with a separating dot or an abbreviated unit word.

vigesimal.label: Counting in scores
vigesimal.note: ˣˣ multiplies by twenty: iiijˣˣ = 4 × 20 = 80 (French quatre-vingts); also found in English accounts.
vigesimal.justification: Score notation is reported as frequent in late-medieval print and characterises some French and British records, with continued use in early modern hands.
vigesimal.where: Especially French and British accounts and some French-language print.

separate.label: Two numbers run together
separate.note: An internal j prompts a split into two candidate numbers. Check the spacing and layout of the source.
separate.justification: This is a transcription aid. The cited sources document final j, while its use here to propose a split is heuristic.

vinculum.label: Bar over a letter
vinculum.justification: Roman multiplication by 1,000 is documented. Compare the distinction-mark reading when the stroke only identifies a number.

frame.label: Framed numeral
frame.note: Bars on three sides multiply by 100,000: |X̅| = 1,000,000.
frame.justification: Roman three-sided frames multiply by 100,000 in rare high-value inscriptions, with no independently dated examples of continued ordinary use in the other bins.
frame.where: Rare Roman inscriptions recording very large numbers, including monetary amounts.

apostrophus.label: Apostrophus
apostrophus.note: Thousands written with I and reversed C: CIↃ = 1000, IↃ = 500, CCIↃↃ = 10,000. Roman, and revived by early modern printers.
apostrophus.justification: Ancient inscriptional signs, Priscian's account around 500 and Renaissance imprints establish use and transmission; the evidence does not establish general popularity.

ignored.label: Unrecognised signs left out
ignored.note: This reading uses the recognised signs. Inspect the omitted text, signs and units before using the value.
ignored.justification: This is a software fallback. The cited sources illustrate signs that require their own interpretation.

minim.label: Possible misreading of minims
minim.note: In handwriting i, n, u and m are built from identical short strokes (minims); n may be a misread ii, m a misread iii.
minim.justification: Similar strokes motivate alternative transcriptions in late medieval and early modern hands, with judgement required for the individual token.
minim.where: Late medieval and early modern manuscript hands, including Secretary and Scottish examples.

ad.label: Year of the Christian era
ad.note: Read as written in AD/CE. Local calendars could start the year at Christmas, the Annunciation or Easter.
ad.justification: The Christian era spreads in the early Middle Ages and becomes ordinary for years in later Western sources, with local differences in year start.

omittedMillennium.label: Thousand left out
omittedMillennium.note: Try adding a thousand to a shortened year. Check the neighbouring text for a written word for “thousand”.
omittedMillennium.justification: The build provisionally allows shortened late medieval and early modern dates. The León fragment is unverified and printed examples sometimes spell out the thousand.

omittedCentury.label: Hundreds left out
omittedCentury.note: Dates written without thousands and hundreds, the century understood: lxxv for 1475 or 1575.
omittedCentury.justification: Late fifteenth-century printed examples include XCij for 1492. Comparable shortened forms can be considered when the source establishes the century.

auc.label: Years from the founding of Rome (AUC)
auc.note: This converter uses the Varronian epoch, in which AUC 1 corresponds to 753 BCE.
auc.justification: The Hadrianic city date is secure and Renaissance humanists and modern scholarship use AUC retrospectively; require the era and epoch to be supplied.

chronogram.label: Chronogram
chronogram.note: Add selected numeral letters in a phrase. Some traditions count W as VV (10).
chronogram.justification: The ratings apply within the genre of deliberate letter-dates. Capitals, colour or size may select the counted letters.
chronogram.where: Especially early modern European maps, medals and inscriptions containing letter-dates.

medievalLetters.label: Alphabetic numeral signs
medievalLetters.note: Local lists assign different values to letters. Consult the letter gloss and the source tradition.
medievalLetters.justification: Glossaries and specialised local traditions give differing values. A selected source profile is necessary.
medievalLetters.where: Palaeographical glossaries and specialised Iberian traditions.

indiction.label: Indiction
indiction.note: Cycle of 15 numbered years. The converter uses the January reckoning, with 1 CE in indiction 4. Other styles change the count at other times of year.
indiction.justification: A 15-year cycle used by medieval chanceries and some later notaries narrows a dated interval when the year-start style is known.
indiction.where: Medieval chanceries and some later notaries, with local start dates.

spanishEra.label: Spanish era
spanishEra.note: Era year 1 corresponds to 38 BCE. Check the document’s era label and transcription, including any crossed X.
spanishEra.justification: Iberian inscriptions and documents use an era counted from 38 BCE with regional end dates.
spanishEra.where: Iberian inscriptions and charters. Abolition dates varied by jurisdiction.

finalJ.label: Final j
finalJ.note: The last i in a group may descend below the line and look like j.
finalJ.justification: A long or descended last i is written j in many later Western hands and in fifteenth-century print.

ordinalMarks.label: Raised ordinal endings
ordinalMarks.note: Raised letters such as ᵒ can indicate a grammatical ending and leave the value unchanged.
ordinalMarks.justification: Raised ordinal endings such as o in date formulae may carry grammar while leaving the numeral value unchanged.

distinctionMarks.label: Distinction marks
distinctionMarks.note: Dots and bars can identify a numeral within text. An overbar used this way leaves its value unchanged.
distinctionMarks.justification: Dots and strokes can distinguish numerals or currency from letters; they are evidence to retain even when they do not modify the value.

clockIIII.label: Four strokes on clock dials
clockIIII.note: IIII is a customary way to mark the fourth hour on a Roman-numeral dial.
clockIIII.justification: Four strokes are the usual form on modern Roman-numeral dials in the cited synthesis, with older clock examples and surviving alternatives.

hybridNumerals.label: Mixed notation
hybridNumerals.note: Words, Arabic digits and unit signs can supply part of a value. Interpret those elements from their context.
hybridNumerals.justification: Some late medieval and early modern examples mix number words, Arabic digits or special units with Roman numeral signs.

earlyFifty.label: Early fifty
earlyFifty.note: The arrow-shaped sign ↆ has the value 50.
earlyFifty.justification: The early arrow-like forms of fifty are distinct from the late six and from L.

lateSix.label: Late six
lateSix.note: The C-like sign ↅ has the value 6.
lateSix.justification: A late-form six appears from the imperial period and in late-antique and early medieval hands; specialised sources disagree on origins and the end of related forms.
